Title: Diving into large-scale congestion with NOTED as a network controller and machine learning-based traffic forecasting
Text:
Diving into large-scale congestion with NOTED as a
network controller and machine learning-based
traffic forecasting
Elisabetta Schneider1,2 and Carmen Misa Moreira1
1CERN - Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire, Esplanade des Particules 1, 1211 Meyrin,
Geneva, Switzerland, IT department CS group - email: firstname.lastname@cern.ch
2ETH Zurich - Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, Zurich, Switzerland - email: eschneider@ethz.ch
Abstract. The Network Optimised Transfer of Experimental Data (NOTED)
has undergone successful testing at several international conferences, includ-
ing the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Network-
ing, Storage and Analysis (also known as SuperComputing). It has also been
tested at scale during the WLCG Data Challenge 2024 (DC24), in which NREN
and WLCG sites conducted testing at 25% of the rates foreseen for the High-
Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). During these events, NOTED has demonstrated
its ability to detect network congestion and dynamically reconfigure the net-
work by executing actions, thereby enhancing network utilisation. Recently,
the integration of NOTED with the CERN’s Network Monitoring System has
increased its ability to detect and respond to congestion in the LHCOPN (Tier
0 to Tier 1’s links) and LHCONE (Tier 1’s to Tier 2’s links) networks. We re-
port here on NOTED’s enhanced ability to identify congested WLCG sites and
DC24 experiences with network reconfiguration to alleviate the detected con-
gestion. Previous work has demonstrated the feasibility of improving NOTED’s
ability to predict network traffic using machine learning with LSTM (Long
Short-Term Memory) networks, given its capacity to learn from historical data.
We present here new findings on the beneficial impact of various encoder-
decoder-based machine learning architectures, including sequence-to-sequence
(Seq2Seq) models, Autoencoders, and Transformers, on NOTED’s performance
in relation to traffic forecasting.
1 Introduction
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments at CERN generate vast amounts of scien-
tific data, leading to significant network traffic. This can sometimes saturate network links,
causing congestion, while alternative paths remain underutilized [1]. To address this issue,
the Network Optimised Transfer of Experimental Data (NOTED) project was introduced in
2020. Its primary goal is to enhance network utilization by better exploiting available band-
width between endpoints. However, traffic engineering with NOTED presents challenges,
particularly when brief periods of congestion do not justify rerouting traffic. Accurate esti-
mation of large data transfer durations is therefore crucial to determine when rerouting can
improve network efficiency and reduce transfer latencies [2].

Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach for accurately estimating network traffic
durations. By incorporating machine learning-based forecasting algorithms specifically de-
signed to predict network congestion patterns and transfer durations, the NOTED architecture
can gain valuable insights to optimize data transfers [3].
To refine NOTED’s predictive capabilities, various machine learning architectures have been
explored for handling time series data. Studies have shown that Long Short-Term Memory
(LSTM) networks, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and hybrid models like CNN-
LSTM and Conv-LSTM are feasible for network traffic forecasting by using NOTED as a
network controller, the results are reported in [3]. Each model leverages its strengths: CNNs
excel in spatial feature extraction, while LSTMs are adept at capturing temporal dependen-
cies. The combination of these architectures has yielded promising results in improving traffic
forecasting accuracy [4]. Ongoing research continues to focus on enhancing the performance
and accuracy of time series prediction.
Encoder-Decoder architectures, particularly those integrating advanced Transformer mod-
els, show significant potential in further advancing traffic forecasting capabilities [5]. These
Encoder-Decoder architectures include the basic sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model,
which processes input sequences into a fixed-size context vector that is subsequently used
to generate the output sequence [6]. While effective in many scenarios, this model can strug-
gle with long-range dependencies. To overcome this limitation, attention mechanisms are
introduced, enabling the model to dynamically focus on different parts of the input sequence
and thus capture more relevant information over longer sequences [7]. Autoencoders, an-
other related architecture, are particularly effective for tasks like time series forecasting by
encoding input data into a lower-dimensional latent space and then decoding it back to its
original form [8] [9]. Transformers take this approach even further by relying entirely on
self-attention mechanisms, eliminating the need for recurrence and enabling parallel process-
ing, which significantly enhances training efficiency and scalability [10] [11].
This paper seeks to compare various Encoder-Decoder architectures—specifically a basic
Seq2Seq model, a Seq2Seq model with an additional attention layer, an Autoencoder, and a
Transformer—in terms of their effectiveness in network traffic forecasting within the NOTED
framework. By evaluating these different models, the paper aims to identify which architec-
ture best enhances the predictive accuracy and computational efficiency of network traffic
forecasting. To provide a comprehensive analysis, the paper is structured as follows. First,
the motivation and objectives driving this study are presented in section 1. Section 2 then out-
lines the machine learning algorithms explored, building the foundation for understanding the
subsequent comparisons. In section 3, the dataset used to train and test these models is intro-
duced, while the results obtained during the comparison are presented in section 4, reflecting
the comprehensive evaluation of the implemented models. Finally, section 5 summarizes the
conclusions and discusses potential directions for future research.
2 Machine Learning Algorithms
This section provides a detailed overview of the machine learning algorithms implemented
in this study, all of which are based on encoder-decoder architectures. The algorithms are
schematically illustrated in Figure 1. All models were implemented in Python 3 by using the
Keras TensorFlow library.

2.1 Seq2Seq Encoder-Decoder Model
A Seq2Seq model consists of an encoder that compresses the input sequence into a fixed-
length context vector and a decoder that generates the output sequence from this vector.
However, this approach can be limiting, particularly with long sequences, as it requires the
model to encode all essential information into one vector. This compression can result in the
loss of important details and reduced performance in generating accurate outputs [12]. To
overcome this limitation, an attention mechanism (AM) is incorporated into the model.
The AM allows the decoder to dynamically focus on different parts of the input sequence
during the output generation process. By assigning higher weights to more relevant or recent
time steps, the attention layer improves prediction accuracy, particularly in scenarios where
future predictions depend on specific, potentially non-contiguous, past periods [13] [14].
2.2 Autoencoder
An Autoencoder is a neural network that identifies patterns and key features within sequences
by compressing them into a latent space that captures dependencies. It is trained to minimize
the difference between the original input and its reconstruction, effectively learning the most
essential features of the data. When applied to historical time series data, an Autoencoder
can reconstruct sequences, capturing important temporal information automatically [15].
Like the Seq2Seq model, an Autoencoder consists of an encoder and a decoder. However,
instead of generating an output sequence from a context vector, the Autoencoder compresses
the input data into a lower-dimensional latent space, from which the decoder reconstructs the
original input [16].
This decoder is then adapted to not only reconstruct the input sequence but also generate
a sequence of future values. In this configuration, the model uses past values encoded by
the encoder to predict future values through the decoder. This is achieved by training the
network with sequences of historical data as inputs and corresponding future sequences as
targets, allowing the Autoencoder to map past data to future predictions [17].

2.3 Transformer
Transformers are deep learning architectures that, unlike traditional Recurrent Neural Net-
works (RNNs) and LSTMs, rely entirely on self-attention mechanisms to process input se-
quences. This self-attention allows Transformers to capture complex dependencies, includ-
ing temporal ones, by focusing on the most relevant parts of the input sequence, making
them particularly useful for tasks like predicting future values. Additionally, Transformers
incorporate positional encoding, which helps the model understand the order of data points,
a critical aspect for time-dependent data [11] [16].
Like Seq2Seq and Autoencoder models, Transformers consist of an encoder and a decoder.
The encoder captures and encodes the input sequence into a detailed representation, while
the decoder generates the output sequence. However, Transformers differ in that their en-
coders and decoders consist of multiple layers, each containing a self-attention mechanism
and a feed-forward neural network, allowing them to handle complex dependencies more
effectively than traditional sequence models [18].
Another distinct feature of Transformers is their flexibility; they can be configured in three
setups: Encoder-Decoder, Encoder-Only, and Decoder-Only [19]. This paper explores both
the Encoder-Only and Encoder-Decoder Transformer configurations.
3 Test Dataset
The machine learning models are trained and tested on a preselected dataset, as shown in
Figure 2, which captures the evolution of four key network traffic parameters over a 16-
hour period for a specific link within the LHCONE (Large Hadron Collider Open Network
Environment) network. This dataset represents real-world data generated by the File Transfer
Service (FTS), a key service employed by LHC experiments to distribute data across various
sites within the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG). The parameters analyzed are the
amount of data transferred [GB], throughput [Gbps], the number of parallel transfers, and the
number of queued transfers.

Highlighted in pink within the figure are periods when the network link became saturated,
as data transfers exceeded the predefined maximum thresholds, which are used to trigger
the alarms, indicated in orange. During these intervals, NOTED triggered an alert, leading
to dynamic reconfiguration of the network to alleviate congestion. This reconfiguration can
involve either provisioning dynamic circuits—adding new network paths through Software-
Defined Networks (SDN) to redistribute traffic—or adjusting BGP configurations to balance
the load across existing links and optimize network utilization, as reported in [2]. The main
objective hereby is to ensure that network traffic, particularly throughput, remains within
the established minimum and maximum thresholds to prevent congestion. To achieve this,
NOTED employs real-time traffic forecasting and uses these predictions to determine whether
action is necessary to optimize network utilization.
To enable accurate throughput predictions, the models must first undergo training. The LH-
CONE dataset is divided into training and testing sets, using a 70-30 split. The training phase,
covering approximately 11.2 hours, focuses on optimizing the models to predict network traf-
fic with high accuracy, particularly by identifying the hyperparameters that minimize the Root
Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for each model. These values are summarized in Table 1. The
subsequent testing phase involves forecasting network traffic over the remaining 4.8 hours,
corresponding to the testing portion of the dataset.
4 Results
Figure 3 presents the forecasting results for each model, with the original LHCONE through-
put data in blue and the training and testing predictions in pink and orange, respectively. Table
2 offers a detailed comparison of the models’ performance in predicting network throughput
over a 4.8-hour period. The performance is assessed by calculating the mean RMSE value
and the corresponding standard deviation (σ(RMSE)) across ten training iterations. Addition-
ally, the Spearman Rank correlation coefficient rs, a non-parametric statistic that evaluates
how well a monotonic relationship describes the connection between two variables without
assuming any specific distribution, is computed to measure the strength of the association
between the actual and estimated traffic [3]. The computational efficiency is evaluated by
measuring the total CPU training time using a 12-core CPU (Apple M2 Max Chip 12-core
CPU: 8 High-Performance Cores and 4 High-Efficiency Cores).
The Seq2Seq Encoder-Decoder model with an attention layer achieved the best predictive
accuracy, with an RMSE of 5.740 and an rs of 0.9780 (highlighted in bold in 2), followed
closely by the basic Seq2Seq model. The Transformer (Encoder-Only) model also demon-
strated strong performance, with an RMSE of 5.904 and the highest rs value of 0.9782, indi-
cating its strong ability to capture the relevant temporal dependencies in the data.
The Autoencoder and Transformer (Encoder-Decoder) models had the highest RMSE at

5 Discussion
The results of this study underscore the significant potential of incorporating advanced
encoder-decoder architectures into the NOTED system for traffic forecasting. Among the
models evaluated, the Seq2Seq model with the additional attention layer demonstrated su-

perior performance, achieving the lowest RMSE and high correlation with actual network
traffic patterns, highlighted in bold in Table 2. This highlights the importance of dynamically
focusing on relevant input sequences to improve predictive accuracy, especially in complex,
time-dependent datasets like network traffic.
The Transformer models, particularly the encoder-only, also showed strong performance,
with the highest Spearman Rank correlation coefficient, indicating a robust ability to maintain
the rank order of predicted values. However, the slightly higher RMSE compared to the
Seq2Seq models suggests that while Transformers excel in capturing complex dependencies,
they may benefit from further fine-tuning or more extensive training data to enhance accuracy.
Interestingly, the Autoencoder, which is often effective in dimensionality reduction and fea-
ture extraction, underperformed in this specific application. Its higher RMSE and lower cor-
relation coefficient indicate that, in the context of network traffic forecasting, the traditional
Autoencoder architecture might not be as well-suited as Seq2Seq or Transformer models.
This could be due to the complexity of the temporal dependencies inherent in the data, which
may require more sophisticated mechanisms like attention or self-attention to capture ef-
fectively. Additionally, the Autoencoder’s latent space representation might have failed to
preserve crucial temporal information, leading to a less accurate model for forecasting tasks
that rely heavily on sequential data.
The computational efficiency analysis further supports the practical application of Seq2Seq
models, which were the fastest to train. This efficiency, combined with their strong per-
formance, makes them a compelling choice for real-time network traffic forecasting within
NOTED. In contrast, the longer training times of the Transformer models, while justifiable
by their accuracy, may pose challenges in scenarios where rapid model updates are required.
Overall, this study demonstrates that while advanced models like Transformers offer promis-
ing capabilities, particularly in handling complex dependencies, Seq2Seq models with at-
tention mechanisms currently provide the best balance of accuracy and efficiency for traffic
forecasting in the NOTED system. Given the time constraint of just a few minutes for real-
time congestion prediction over a 20-30 minute window, reducing training duration is more
critical than achieving the highest possible accuracy. Therefore, in our specific case, the
model we choose is not only one of the most accurate but also one of the fastest, ensuring
timely predictions that meet the operational requirements of the NOTED system. Future work
could explore applying these models across different network links to test their generalizabil-
ity. Being able to train one model that works for all the links in the LHCONE and LHCOPN
networks would be the ultimate goal. Additionally, incorporating more extensive datasets or
leveraging transfer learning could further enhance the performance of these models in real-
world applications.
